lessons.title: Planned maintenance of poultry houses and equipment
lessons.html:
Why maintenance is a bird welfare issue

In a poultry house, equipment keeps birds alive. If fans stop on a hot afternoon or the water pump fails at night, birds can die within hours. Maintenance is therefore not something to do when there is time. It must be planned, scheduled and checked.

What needs maintenance

  • Ventilation: fans, belts, shutters, curtains, inlets, cooling pads and controllers.
  • Heating: gas brooders and heaters, pipes, regulators and gas leaks.
  • Water: pumps, tanks, filters, regulators, nipple lines and drinkers.
  • Feed: silos, augers, motors, feeder pans and level sensors.
  • Power: generator, change-over switch, distribution boards, lights and alarms.
  • Structure: roofs, walls, doors, wire mesh, floors and drainage.

Types of maintenance

Daily checks are done by house staff: are fans running, lines working, alarms on? Planned preventive maintenance follows a calendar, for example tightening fan belts monthly, servicing the generator by hours run and calibrating temperature probes each cycle. Between-flock maintenance uses the empty period for bigger jobs such as repairing floors, replacing worn nipple lines and fixing curtains. Breakdown repairs happen when something fails; good planning makes these rare.

Running the maintenance system

  1. Keep an equipment register for each house.
  2. Draw up a maintenance schedule from the manufacturers' manuals.
  3. Issue job cards, record what was done, parts used and cost.
  4. Hold critical spares on site: fan belts, a spare pump, fuses, nipples and regulators.
  5. Review breakdowns monthly to find repeat failures.

Safety during maintenance

Under the OHS Act 85 of 1993 the employer must provide safe working conditions. Isolate and lock out electrical equipment before working on fans or augers. Never put hands into a running auger. Use a safe ladder or platform for roof and silo work, and never climb silos alone. Check gas fittings with soapy water, never with a flame.

lessons.title: Physical biosecurity barriers and controls
lessons.html:
Keeping disease out

Physical biosecurity is the set of barriers that stop disease from getting onto the farm and into the houses. Diseases such as avian influenza and Newcastle disease can wipe out a flock and lead to quarantine of the farm. As supervisor, you must keep the barriers in good order and make sure everyone uses them.

The farm perimeter

  • A fence and one controlled gate, kept locked.
  • A visitors' register: name, date, reason, and the last poultry contact.
  • Vehicle wheel dip or spray at the gate, with disinfectant mixed and changed as the label says.
  • Parking for visitors outside the clean area.

The house entrance

  • A changing room with a clear line between dirty and clean sides.
  • Shower-in or at least hand wash and change into farm clothes and boots.
  • Footbaths at every house door, kept topped up and clean. A footbath full of mud does not work.
  • Separate boots and tools for each house where possible.

Keeping out wild birds, rodents and pests

Wild birds carry avian influenza. Check that mesh on curtains and openings has no holes, doors close properly and feed spills are cleaned up. Run a rodent control programme with bait stations placed and numbered on a map, checked and recorded regularly. Keep the area around houses mown and free of rubbish. Control flies and beetles in litter.

Cleaning and disinfection between flocks

  1. Remove all birds, then all litter and manure.
  2. Dry clean, then wash with detergent from top to bottom.
  3. Disinfect with a registered product at the label rate.
  4. Clean the water lines and feed system.
  5. Fix maintenance items while the house is empty.
  6. Allow drying and the planned down time before placing.

Never mix chemicals unless the label allows it, and wear the PPE stated on the label.

Key points

  • Equipment failure can kill birds quickly, so maintenance must be planned.
  • Keep an equipment register, schedule and critical spares.
  • Lock out power before working on fans or augers.
  • Fences, gates, registers, footbaths and changing rooms must be kept working.
  • Clean and disinfect fully between flocks and allow down time.

Because it is required for egg colour

quiz.question: When is the best time for big jobs like replacing nipple lines and repairing floors?

options.text: In the empty period between flocks

quiz.question: How should gas fittings be checked for leaks?

options.text: By smelling only once a year

quiz.question: What should be done before working on a fan or feed auger?

options.text: Ask a worker to hold the switch
Isolate and lock out the electrical supply

quiz.question: What is the correct order for cleaning a house between flocks?

options.text: Disinfect, then remove litter, then wash
Remove birds and litter, wash with detergent, then disinfect
Place new chicks, then clean around them

Wild birds can carry avian influenza, so holes in curtain mesh must be repaired.
